newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore assures China in funds row, sees rosy future.
newsitem.headline: Gore assures China in funds row, sees rosy future.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore said on Wednesday a probe into allegations of illegal funding to the Democratic Party by Beijing should not disrupt China-U.S. ties but proof of payments would make this a serious matter.
Gore, winding up two days of talks with Chinese leaders, also said U.S. officials had brought up specific cases of human rights questions during his visit.

"The discussions of the (payments) controversy now, pending the completion of the investigation should not affect the relationship between China and the United States," Gore told reporters after two days of meetings with Chinese leaders.
"I... said that the U.S. views these allegations as very serious, however, they're the subject of an ongoing criminal investigation in our Justice Department," he said.
"It is premature to speculate on what the outcome of that investigation is," he said.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign funds from foreign corporations.
Gore said the issue did not come up in a meeting with President Jiang Zemin on Wednesday but was raised with Premier Li Peng on Tuesday. Li had denied the allegations vigorously.
Asked if he believed the Chinese denial, Gore said: "I am not in a position to judge."
Turning to human rights, another thorny issue in Sino-U.S. ties, Gore said: "Specific cases were raised during the course of my visit."

However, he did not identify dissidents who were mentioned by him or other U.S. officials in talks since he arrived on Monday, the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit China since Beijing's 1989 crackdown on student demonstrations.
"I am not going to specify individual names," he said.
The Chinese were more receptive to the U.S. position than they had been in the past, he said.
Asked how he had reached that conclusion, he said the more receptive response was reflected in "the language that was used, the muted tone of the response" compared with past reactions.
China has intensified police surveillance around its tiny community of dissidents to prevent contacts with U.S. officials during Gore's visit, and even moved some out of Beijing.
Gore clearly wanted to prevent such sensitive topics as human rights, trade, Taiwan and arms proliferation casting a shadow over efforts to repair badly strained Sino-U.S. ties.
"Our discussions were productive, friendly, searching and above all wide-ranging," Gore said of his meeting with Jiang.
The two sides reaffirmed their commitment for Jiang to visit the United States in the autumn of this year and officials of both sides were beginning work on setting dates.
President Bill Clinton is expected to visit China in 1998.
Jiang, who is also chief of China's ruling Communist Party, greeted Gore in upbeat style before the meeting, saying his visit had been very productive.
Gore said the United States expected China to live up to its commitments on Hong Kong after the transfer of power on July 1. "We expect China to honour its commitments," he said.

The Sino-British accord reached in 1984 calls for the capitalist system and structure of the booming territory to remain unchanged for 50 years after the British colony reverts to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30.
